# A working coursebook {.unnumbered}

This book follows a long-term project to understand modern language models through mathematics, implementation, experiments, and research. Its destination is practical: read a model's paper and source code, trace its computations, derive its central equations, and implement a smaller version.

The chapters grow out of the learning sessions. Each brings together the explanation, exercises, worked solutions, and the reasoning developed while doing them. A chapter may be recorded in parts while its unit is still in progress.

::: {.callout-note title="Start here"}
[Unit 1: Derivatives as predictions of local change](units/01-local-change.qmd) is complete. It develops scalar derivatives, gradients, directional derivatives, and a first gradient-descent update.

[Unit 2: Computational graphs and the multivariable chain rule](units/02-computational-graphs.qmd) is complete. It organizes calculations into graphs, follows derivatives through shared values, and derives a nonlinear neuron's backward pass.

[Unit 3: Scalar automatic differentiation](units/03-scalar-autodiff.qmd) is complete. It implements local backward rules, handles shared values, and assembles an automatic reverse traversal in Python.

[Unit 4: Vector and matrix derivatives](units/04-vector-matrix-derivatives.qmd) is complete. It develops backward rules for batched affine layers, elementwise activations, and sum and mean reductions. The final checkpoint traces a scalar loss back through a batched layer and shows how to compute the gradients directly.
:::

## Reading this book

The website includes interactive figures and expandable solutions. Try an exercise before opening its solution; then compare the reasoning, not just the final number.

The coursebook is currently published as a website. Interactive figures let you change parameters or step through a backward pass, and code examples can be copied for local experiments.

## The route ahead

| Milestone | Main question | Practical work |
|---|---|---|
| Learning mechanics | How do we calculate and use the gradient of a loss? | Derive and verify a small network's backward pass |
| Probabilistic prediction | What does a language model estimate, and why this training objective? | Build a simple next-token model |
| Transformers | How does attention turn a token sequence into predictions? | Implement a compact causal transformer |
| Training in practice | What makes a training run succeed or fail? | Run controlled experiments |
| A modern architecture | How do real model configurations connect to equations and code? | Reproduce selected components at smaller dimensions |
| Assistants and inference | How do training, decoding, memory, and tools shape behavior? | Inspect real inference and assistant workflows |

This is a flexible route. Topics receive more detail as we approach them. Understanding public architectures and methods is achievable; explaining every behavior of a trained model also touches open research.

## A recurring learning cycle

1. Ask a concrete question.
2. Develop the intuition and derive the mathematics.
3. Implement or calculate a small example.
4. Check the result independently.
5. Record what is understood and what remains uncertain.

The mathematics will mainly draw on linear algebra, multivariable calculus, probability, and optimization. Selected book passages provide deeper treatments when needed; see the [reading references](reference.qmd).
